analysis.one_liner: Reinstates excise taxes on oil and toxic chemicals to make polluters fund toxic-site cleanups.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past the Senate Finance Committee, dying there with a single sponsor and no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have brought back the Superfund 'polluter pays' taxes that expired in 1995: a per-barrel fee on crude oil and new per-ton fees on dozens of toxic chemicals like benzene, mercury, and arsenic. The money goes into the Superfund trust fund, which pays to clean up the nation's worst hazardous waste sites. The fees would rise with inflation through 2018. It never got a committee hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near or downstream from hazardous waste sites, who get faster and better-funded cleanups, and ordinary taxpayers generally, who currently bear the cleanup costs that polluting industries shifted to the public when the fees lapsed in 1995.

how_it_helps.text: The bill reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate, which expired at the end of 1995, so money for toxic waste cleanups again comes from the oil and chemical companies whose products create the hazard rather than from general taxpayers.

It raises the crude oil financing rate from 9.7 cents to 17.0 cents per barrel and imposes per-ton excise taxes on dozens of hazardous chemicals, with both adjusted for inflation through 2018 so the fund does not quietly shrink.
It also raises the existing environmental excise tax on certain chemicals sold by their manufacturers, producers, and importers, broadening the base of industries paying into cleanup.
Technical changes remove tax breaks for exported crude oil and chemicals, so the fees apply to the substances actually used here.

analysis.who_pays: Oil refiners and petrochemical manufacturers, whose per-barrel and per-ton fees would rise; some of that cost would likely pass through to prices of gasoline and chemical-based products.

drawbacks.text: The fees are passed down the supply chain, so some of the cost would show up in prices for gasoline, plastics, and other chemical-derived goods that ordinary households buy.

The chemical fee table sets fixed dollar amounts per substance that may not track the actual hazard or cleanup cost of each chemical, an imperfect match between what a company pays and the harm its products cause.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: a modest per-unit fee on oil and toxic chemicals in exchange for a cleanup fund that would otherwise be paid for by general taxpayers. The pass-through to consumer prices is real but small per household, and the fee structure is crude in places. On balance the bill shifts a public burden back onto the industries that create it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Nelson introduced the Superfund Polluter Pays Act on March 16, 2010, the day the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No further action was ever recorded; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
No senator cosponsored the bill, so it went into committee with the minimum possible support.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil refiners and petrochemical manufacturers benefit, because the fees that would have made them pay into toxic-site cleanups never took effect; the cleanup burden stays with general taxpayers.

for.name: Sen. Bill Nelson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or a vote on the bill in the nearly two years remaining in the Congress.

against.name: Chemical and petroleum industry
against.role: Industries that would pay the reinstated excise taxes
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against reinstating the Superfund taxes after they lapsed in 1995; the taxes remained unfunded throughout this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote, so no party positions were recorded; it had one Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of any party.

industries.industry: Oil refiners and crude oil producers
industries.note: The bill reinstates and nearly doubles the per-barrel Superfund fee on crude oil, from 9.7 to 17 cents, and removes a tax break for exported crude. Refiners currently benefit from the fee's absence because taxpayers fund site cleanups instead.

The bill sets per-ton excise taxes on dozens of toxic chemicals, from benzene to mercury, payable by their manufacturers, producers, and importers, and raises some existing chemical taxes. These companies' products generate much of the hazardous waste the Superfund cleans up.
A replenished Superfund trust fund means more federally funded cleanup work, which goes to environmental remediation firms. More cleanups also mean less toxic exposure for nearby residents.
